newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian MP assailed over expense claims.
newsitem.headline: Australian MP assailed over expense claims.

text.p: The Australian government faced mounting pressure on Tuesday to take action over charges that a key independent senator had abused his parliamentary perks as a scandal over false travel claims deepened.

The national police union urged Prime Minister John Howard to launch an official police investigation into senator Mal Colston, saying the high-profile affair had become politicised and only an independent probe could clear the air.
"Nobody knows what to believe as a result of this contrived environment of media frenzy and political point-scoring," said police union chief Chris Eaton.

Colston, a Labor opposition defector now sitting as an independent in the upper house Senate, has been accused of claiming travel allowances when he was at home, misusing his postal allowance and abusing other parliamentary perks.
Separately, Attorney-General Daryl Williams announced that a government parliamentarian and a recently retired colleague would be charged with fraud over travel and car claims.
Lower house National Party MP Michael Cobb and former Liberal senator Bob Woods, who both deny any wrongdoing, will face court at a later date.

Howard, who led the conservative Liberal-National alliance to power a year ago after 13 years in opposition, has pledged to lift parliamentary standards and restore public confidence in politicians and implemented a new code of conduct.

But the Colston affair has been a thorn in his side for six weeks. Political opponents, former staffers and at least one family member have charged Colston everything from the illegal to the comic in a saga that has dominated political coverage.

Among the accusations is that Colston held a chauffer-driven car outside a local supermarket until midnight to buy chicken at half price, asked the parliamentary library to do his son's university work, flew across the country and back to amass frequent flyer points and gave another woman a parliamentary travel pass issued in his wife's name.
Colston, the Senate's deputy president and one of two independents the government has relied on to pass its legislation in the upper house, has denied any wrongdoing.
But he repaid A$6,880 (US$5,300) last month after a Senate inquiry found he had wrongly claimed 43 days of travel allowances in less than four years. He blamed a book-keeping error by an employee.
The government said on Tuesday it would wait for a departmental probe before deciding whether to call in police.

Labor, which has vowed revenge on Colston for "ratting" on the party, has accused Howard of buying his support with the deputy presidency and extra perks for his staff. Howard and Colston dismiss the charges as spiteful.
Meanwhile newspaper cartoonists have delighted in portraying the corpulent, shuffling senator from conservative Queensland as a pig with his snout in the public trough.
Labor and minor leftist parties have demanded Colston quit.
Labor tactician Robert Ray, leading the anti-Colston crusade, openly admits the party is out for revenge.
"Anyone who rats on the Labor Party will get exactly what that quisling Quasimodo from Queensland got," he said.
If police investigated the Colston charges and he were convicted of fraud, he could no longer sit in the Senate.
That would throw the fate of future government legislation, including its 1997/98 budget, into doubt because he would be replaced by a Labor member as he was elected as a Labor member.
